Directions: In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Professionalism is probably the _____ (A) theoretical of the types of soft skills, and certainly the most dependent on context. What professionalism ______ (B) in one organization can be very different from what it means in another. In general, what most employers mean when they say they are _______ (C) for professionalism is someone who understands how they as an individual affect the ______ (D) as a whole. That can mean anything from personal performance related to broad standards, or how one's ______ (E) impacts the health of the team.

Select the appropriate word to fill blank A.
p75mock001.explanation:
The blank requires an adverb that is in Superlative degree to qualify the adjective 'theoretical' as the sentence denotes 'professionalism' is the ultimatum of the soft skills. 'Less' is in a positive degree while 'more' and 'lesser' are in comparative degrees which can be used when two objects are in comparison. Since that is not the context of the sentence, they are negated. 'Most' which means 'forming the superlative of adjectives and adverbs, especially those of more than one syllable' is the appropriate adverb in the superlative form that can qualify the adjective 'theoretical' in the context of the given sentence.

Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

Note:

Qualifiers: A word or phrase that limits the meaning of another word or phrase or makes it less general. 'Adverbs' and 'adjectives' are qualifiers.

· The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

· The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

· The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.

'Explains' (give a reason so as to justify or excuse (an action or event)) and 'ignored' (refuse to take notice of or acknowledge; disregard intentionally) are contextually irrelevant words as 'professionalism' cannot do these two actions in the context of an organization, so they are negated. 'Avoiding' is in a continuous form that does not have an auxiliary verb to support it, so it is also negated. 'Means' (intend to convey or refer to (a particular thing); signify) is the most appropriate word that indicates the role of professionalism in the given context of the sentence.

Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

Note:

Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'.

The verb has to be either in Past participle form (V3) or continuous/present participle form (V4) to be used along with the auxiliary verb 'are'. 'Reward' and 'expect' are in base forms of the verbs (V1), so they are negated. 'Awarding' (give or order the giving of (something) as an official payment, compensation, or prize to (someone)) is a contextually irrelevant option as it makes the sentence meaningless if used, so it is negated. 'Looking' when used along with the preposition 'for' means 'hope or expect to find or obtain a particular type of person or thing' and indicates the thing that employers do with respect to professionalism in a person.

Hence, the correct answer is option (d).

Note:

Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'.

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence.

Examples

I. The teacher scolded the child for being late.

II. We're going to a party.

· The words in bold are called prepositions because they normally take a position before (pre) a noun/pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition.

· The noun/pronoun which is used with a preposition is called its Object.

Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.

(a) For comprehensive understanding of complex subjects,

(b) and consistent review of material

(c) active participation in discussions,

(d) are absolutely essential for students

(e) diligent note-taking during lectures,
p75mock001.explanation:
(a) For comprehensive understanding of complex subjects, - This introductory prepositional phrase sets the context or purpose for what follows. It indicates why the subsequent actions are necessary.

(c) active participation in discussions, - This is the first item in a list of essential actions or requirements that form the compound subject of the sentence. It follows the introductory phrase: "For comprehensive understanding of complex subjects, active participation in discussions,"

(e) diligent note-taking during lectures, - This is the second item in the list of essential actions, parallel in structure to (c). It continues the enumeration: "...active participation in discussions, diligent note-taking during lectures,"

(b) and consistent review of material - This is the third and final item in the list, connected by the conjunction "and." It completes the compound subject: "...diligent note-taking during lectures, and consistent review of material"

(d) are absolutely essential for students - This is the predicate of the sentence, with "are" agreeing with the plural compound subject (participation, note-taking, and review), and "absolutely essential for students" explaining their importance.

Final sentence: "For comprehensive understanding of complex subjects, active participation in discussions, diligent note-taking during lectures, and consistent review of material are absolutely essential for students."

Hence, option (a) is the answer.

p75mock001.word: Select the correct sentence in passive voice from the following options.
options: The maid has been cleaning the house.
The maid is cleaning the house.
The maid has cleaned the house.
The house has been cleaned by the maid.
p75mock001.explanation:
In passive voice, the subject of the sentence receives the action rather than performing it. Option (d) is the correct passive voice sentence because the subject (the house) is receiving the action (being cleaned) by the maid. The maid is not the subject here; instead, she is the one doing the action, which is cleaning the house. Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

The rest of the options are in the active voice.

p75mock001.word:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The skill has been perfected by my mentor. I have been shaped by my mentor since my adulthood.
options: My mentor has perfected the skill. Since my adulthood, my mentor has shaped me.
My mentor has been perfected the skill. Since my adulthood, my mentor has shaped me.
My mentor has perfected the skill. Since my adulthood, my mentor have shaped me.
My mentor is perfected the skill. Since my adulthood, my mentor having shaped me.
p75mock001.explanation:
The subject of the Passive Voice is changed into the object of the Active Voice. Also, the object of the Passive Voice is changed into the subject of the Active Voice.

The removal of the "to be" verb ('been' in this case) and the preposition 'by' is necessary while changing the voice of the sentence from Passive to Active.

The Passive voice in this question is in Present Perfect tense. Thus, the Active voice will also be in Present Perfect.

In Passive voice, the format is: Object of the Active voice (Subjective case) + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject of the Active voice (Objective case).

Thus, the format of Active voice is: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object.

For example:

A new horse has been bought by Arya. (Passive Voice)

Arya has bought a new horse. (Active Voice)

The options except (a) don't follow the correct grammatical format of the Active Voice.

Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

Note:

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

options: David told me that he had been reading a book when I called him the previous day.
David told me that he was reading a book when I called him the previous day.

p75mock001.explanation:
Option (b) is the correct answer.

If the sentence is in Simple Past, the form of tense doesn't change when it is used in the time clause.

One way of identifying the time clause is that the Time clause always begins with the following: When, whenever, while, as, since, after, before, until, as soon as

For example:

Ayush said to me, "When I saw him, he was working." (Direct Speech)

Ayush told me that when he saw him, he was working. (Indirect Speech)

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:

· The reporting verb 'said to' is changed into 'told'.

· The pronouns 'I' into 'he', 'you' into 'I', and 'me' into 'him' are changed.

· 'Yesterday' is changed into 'the previous day'.

Therefore, the correct answer is option (b): David told me that he was reading a book when I called him the previous day.

Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.

The reason for the unexpected project delay is because the main supplier failed to deliver the crucial components on the agreed-upon date, causing a major logistical bottleneck.
options: is due to the main supplier
is on account of the main supplier
p75mock001.explanation:
The phrase "The reason... is because" is a common redundancy in English. The word "reason" implies causality, as does the word "because." Using them together is grammatically superfluous. The correct construction is "The reason is that..." where "that" introduces a noun clause explaining the reason.

Option a) is that the main supplier correctly replaces "because" with "that," eliminating the redundancy and forming a grammatically sound sentence.

Option b) is due to the main supplier is also problematic. "Due to" should typically modify a noun, not follow a linking verb like "is" in this structure. For example, "The delay was due to the supplier's failure."

Option c) is on account of the main supplier is grammatically possible but wordy and less direct than "is that...". Also, it would need to be followed by the -ing form of verb "failing".

So, the correct sentence is: The reason for the unexpected project delay is that the main supplier failed to deliver the crucial components on the agreed-upon date, causing a major logistical bottleneck.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is a) is that the main supplier.

Honesty and integrity is basic principles in building trust with others.
p75mock001.explanation:
The option that can substitute the underlined segment is 'are fundamental principles'. The original sentence is grammatically incorrect due to subject-verb agreement issues. The subject of the sentence is "Honesty and integrity," which is a compound subject joined by "and." Therefore, it is plural and requires the plural verb "are," not the singular verb "is."

Option (c) rectifies the original error as it uses "are," which agrees with the plural subject and appropriately describes the importance of honesty and integrity in building trust.

Option (a) uses "is," which does not agree with the plural subject "Honesty and integrity."

Option (b) uses "has," which is singular and does not agree with the plural subject. Hence, (c) is the correct answer.

The correct sentence is: Honesty and integrity are fundamental principles in building trust with others.

NOTE:

Subject-verb agreement means that a subject and its verb must be both singular or plural:

A singular subject takes a singular verb.

A plural subject takes a plural verb.

For example, in the sentence 'John lives in France', the subject John (singular 'he') 'agrees with' the third person singular form of the verb to live - lives.

Directions :Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

King Sagara, an ancestor of King Bhagiratha, once conducted an ashwamedha yagna to extend his dominion. When the horse went astray, the king sent his 60,000 sons to find the horse. Unfortunately, in the course of the quest, they ended up disrupting the intense meditation of sage Kapila, at whose abode they found the horse. Kapila burnt them all to ashes, sending them all to the netherworld - an act he instantly regretted when he realised what had happened. After breaking the news to King Sagara, he mentioned that the souls of King Sagara's sons could attain salvation only if the heavenly Ganga could be persuaded to flow over their ashes. It was Bhagiratha, whose austere penance and devotion pleased Lord Shiva so much so that he persuaded Ganga to descend to the earth. Ganga consented, but the problem arose that the earth would probably be unable to bear the intensity of Ganga's flow and even be shattered in the process. Thus, a solution was devised: Ganga would first land on Shiva's head and the locks of his hair would minimise the impact. Still, the force of Ganga's landing was such that it split into seven tributaries, three of which flowed east and three of them west. The seventh stream followed King Bhagiratha to the place where his ancestor's ashes lay. The river's waters instantly purified them. This is also the origin of the belief that the Ganga's waters can purify mortal souls of all their sins.

Identify the option that arranges the given events in the correct sequence of their occurence.

A. King Sagara's sons were burnt by sage Kapila.

B. King Bhagiratha persuaded Ganga to flow to the earth.

C. King Sagara performed an ashwamedha yagna.

D. The souls of the dead sons would not get salvation until Ganga flowed over their ashes.

E. However, the flow had to be restrained by Shiva by holding it in his locks.
p75mock001.explanation:
· C. King Sagara performed an ashwamedha yagna: This is the first event, as the passage begins with King Sagara conducting the ashwamedha yagna, which sets the story in motion when the horse goes astray.

· A. King Sagara's sons were burnt by sage Kapila: After the horse goes missing, Sagara's 60,000 sons search for it, disrupt sage Kapila's meditation, and are burnt to ashes by him.

· D. The souls of the dead sons would not get salvation until Ganga flowed over their ashes: Following the burning, sage Kapila informs King Sagara that the souls of his sons can only attain salvation if the Ganga flows over their ashes.

· B. King Bhagiratha persuaded Ganga to flow to the earth: Much later, King Bhagiratha, an ancestor of Sagara, performs penance to persuade Ganga to descend to earth to purify the ashes.

· E. However, the flow had to be restrained by Shiva by holding it in his locks: To prevent Ganga's flow from shattering the earth, Shiva restrains it in his hair locks before it reaches the earth and splits into tributaries.

Correct Sequence: The events occur in the order C, A, D, B, E:

· Sagara's yagna (C) leads to the sons' search and burning (A).

· Kapila's statement about salvation via Ganga (D) follows.

· Bhagiratha's persuasion of Ganga (B) comes next.

· Shiva restraining Ganga's flow (E) is the final step before the river reaches the ashes.

When Arvind accepted the managerial position at a declining textile firm, he was aware that the challenge extended far beyond falling profits. The company’s real ailment lay buried in its culture—an unspoken resistance to accountability that had slowly normalized mediocrity. Employees met deadlines just well enough to avoid reprimand, innovation was quietly discouraged under the guise of “practicality,” and senior leadership equated stability with stagnation. Arvind initially chose restraint over disruption, believing that trust must precede transformation. However, this cautious approach was soon misinterpreted as indecision, reinforcing the very complacency he intended to dismantle.

As months passed, subtle patterns emerged. Suggestions were applauded in meetings but ignored in execution, data was selectively presented to justify inaction, and failures were attributed to external forces rather than internal inefficiencies. Arvind realized that the organization did not lack talent; it lacked the discomfort necessary for growth. When he finally introduced performance-linked evaluations and transparent reporting mechanisms, resistance intensified. Critics accused him of eroding harmony and imposing corporate rigidity on a “family-like” workplace. Yet beneath these objections lay a deeper fear—the loss of anonymity in collective failure. The turning point came not through dramatic reform but through consistency. Arvind refused to reverse decisions despite mounting pressure, yet he also resisted authoritarian impulses. Over time, clarity replaced confusion. While some employees exited, others adapted, discovering that accountability, though unsettling, offered professional dignity. The firm did not transform overnight, nor did it achieve spectacular success. But it shed its illusion of comfort, replacing it with a fragile yet honest culture—one where progress was measured not by immediate results, but by the willingness to confront inconvenient truths.

The central theme of the passage is:
options: Organizational decline is primarily caused by ineffective leadership decisions
Accountability often disrupts workplace harmony more than inefficiency does
Cultures of comfort can suppress growth by avoiding responsibility
Long-term success requires strict enforcement of performance metrics
p75mock001.explanation:
The Correct Answer is - Cultures of comfort can suppress growth by avoiding responsibility.

Explanation:
The passage consistently shows how comfort, harmony, and stability masked inefficiency and discouraged growth. True progress began only when accountability replaced the illusion of comfort.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG:
A oversimplifies the issue by blaming leadership alone.
B misrepresents the argument, as harmony itself is shown to be superficial.
D exaggerates the role of metrics, which are secondary to cultural change.

options: The photocopier will collate the documents for you.

The photocopier is collating the documents for you.
The photocopier has collated the documents for you.
p75mock002.explanation:
The correct option that expresses the given sentence in future tense form is (a). Option (a) changes the verb "collates" (present tense) to "will collate" (simple future tense). The future tense is used to talk about actions or events that will happen after the present moment. The tense used in option (a) is the simple future tense. It is formed using the auxiliary verb "will" followed by the base form of the main verb (in this case, "collate"). Option (b) is in the simple past tense, which is formed using the "second" form of the verb. Option (c) is in the present continuous tense, which is formed using "is" + the present participle of the verb. Option (d) is in the present perfect tense, which is formed using "has" + past participle of the verb. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Auxiliary verb: A verb that gives grammatical information that is not given by the main verb of a sentence. It supports the main verb. Auxiliary verbs help to form the various tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs. The principal ones are be, do, and have. Example: She will sing a song tomorrow. Here, 'will' is the auxiliary verb that supports the main verb 'sing'.

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

Key Points

  • Eliminating Incorrect Options:

p75mock004.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: The sick admitted in the hospital are receiving
timely treatment, but some sick has not been
attended properly due to shortage of staff.
p75mock004.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option B.

Replace "has" with "have".

Rule/Concept: Nouns that look like adjectives (Adjective-like Nouns)

Some words like sick, poor, rich, young, blind are Nouns even though they often describe a group like adjectives. When they are plural in meaning or refer to multiple people, the verb must agree with the plural sense.

Application to the Given Question: "but some sick has not been attended properly due to shortage of staff."

Here, some sick refers to multiple patients, so the verb must be plural → "have" instead of "has".

Corrected Sentence: but some sick have not been attended properly due to shortage of staff.

More Examples for Clarity:

The poor have been given relief during the flood.

The blind are often ignored in public transport.

The young aspire to excel in competitive exams.

Incorrect Usage:

The rich has donated money for charity.

The sick was waiting for hours in the hospital.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips:

Always identify if the word is acting as a Noun (even if it looks like an Adjective).

Check subject-verb agreement carefully; plural sense → plural verb.

In SSC CGL, this is a common trap in Spot the Error questions.

Hence, option (b) is correct.

NOTE/-

Subjective/Nominative Pronouns: The pronouns I, you, we, he, she, it, and they are known as subjective pronouns because they act as the subjects of verbs: We went to the party.

Objective Pronouns: The pronouns me, you, us, him, her, it, and them are called objective pronouns because they act as the objects of verbs and prepositions: Anjali drove us home.

Possessive Pronouns: The pronouns mine, yours, hers, his, ours, and theirs are known as possessive pronouns: they refer to something owned by the speaker or by someone or something previously mentioned. For example: The pen is mine.

Possessive Determiners/Adjectives: Words like 'my', 'our', 'your', 'his', 'her', 'its', and 'their' are known as possessive adjectives (or possessive determiners). They come before nouns and indicate ownership of the noun. Example: "The teacher asked the students to open their drawing books."

📌 Rule / Concept: Overtake vs. Take over

These terms are frequently confused because they both involve a change in status or position, but their applications are distinct:

Overtake: To catch up with and pass someone or something (physically, numerically, or in terms of progress). It is used for competition, speed, or growth (e.g., "The runner overtook his rival").

Take over: To assume control, command, or possession of something. It is used for management, responsibilities, or business acquisitions (e.g., "The company was taken over by a giant corporation").

It does not mean the emerging economy is "assuming control" or "managing" the developed nations. Since it is a matter of surpassing a benchmark, overtake is the correct term.

More Examples for Clarity -

p75mock007.word: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
options: We must found a solution to this problem before it gets worse.
We must prioritises customer satisfaction in our business strategy.
They will start their journey early to avoid traffic.
He will called you as soon as he gets home from work.
p75mock007.explanation:
The sentence given in option (c) is grammatically correct. This sentence uses the future tense ("will start") appropriately to indicate a future action.

Option (a) is not correct. After the modal verb "must," we use the base form of the verb ("find"). But 'found' (past tense form) is not the base form. Modal verbs like "must" express necessity or obligation and are always followed by the base form of the main verb. So, 'found' should be replaced with the base form 'find'. The correct sentence is: We must find a solution to this problem before it gets worse.

Option (b) is not correct. After the modal verb "must," we use the base form of the verb ("prioritise"). But 'prioritises' (present tense form) is not the base form. Modal verbs such as "must" indicate necessity and are followed by the base form of the verb that expresses the action required. So, 'prioritises' should be replaced with the base form 'prioritise'. The correct sentence is: We must prioritise customer satisfaction in our business strategy.

Option (d) is incorrect as well. After the modal verb "will," we use the base form of the verb ("call"). Modal verbs like "will" express future actions or intentions and are followed by the base form of the main verb. But 'called' (past tense form) is not the base form. So, we should replace 'called' with the base form 'call'. The correct sentence is: He will call you as soon as he gets home from work. Hence, (c) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Modal verb: A verb used with another verb to express an idea such as possibility that is not expressed by the main verb. The modal verbs in English are "can," "could," "may," "might," "must," "ought," "shall," "should," "will," and "would." They do not change their form (spelling) and they have no infinitive or participle (past/present). Example: I can speak Spanish. Here 'can' expresses the ability of the person to speak (main verb) Spanish. This ability cannot be expressed by the main verb 'speak'.

The mayor _____ plans to revitalize the downtown area and _____ more businesses.

According to the subject-verb agreement rule, we cannot use the plural verb 'revitalize' (imbue (something) with new life and vitality) with the singular subject 'mayor'. So, option (b) is eliminated. The present participle verb 'attracting' doesn't fit in the first position as it requires a helping verb before it which is not there. So, option (c) is eliminated. The complete sentence is: The mayor announced plans to revitalize the downtown area and attract more businesses.

Note:

Subject-Verb Agreement: Matching up singular or plural subjects with singular or plural forms of a verb is part of the process called agreement. This can be understood better by the examples given: - "She likes cooking." [singular subject and verb] -- "They like to cook vegetables." [plural subject and verb]

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

I asked if I could use the phone in his study and she said I could." At this point my companion, attentive as ever, offered her second assumption of the evening, and though more likely than the first, it was just as wrong: "And he never called and that's why you hate phones." No, that's not why. "When mother told me he was on the line, I rushed to the study and dropped the needle on Nulla in Mundo Pax Sincera, then picked up the phone. He didn't say hello or ask how I was, he only said that there's no peace in the world. He'd looked, it wasn't there, not for him." With her final assumption, she came closer to the truth: "So phones remind you of your father, and that's why you hate them."

"That's part of it," I said, "but there's more. He said he could hear Vivaldi in the background and told me to keep listening, that aria was on to something. Then he said goodbye to me and mother and everyone else. Forever. He found his peace." The music prevented a silence that would've felt more comfortable, then it finally stopped and I let the silence prevail. And there we sat, speaking without speaking, until the silence was shattered by a ring. I stood and walked to the phone, picked it up, not just the receiver, but all of it, and paused to admire the artistry.

For example:

She will have bought the gold. (Active Voice)

The gold will have been bought by her. (Passive Voice)

The teacher will never / give you punishment / if you will / come on time.
p75mock010.explanation: The error is in the segment "if you will." In English, the simple present tense is used in conditional clauses introduced by "if" when referring to future possibilities, not the future tense with "will." The correct form is "if you come on time." Thus, the sentence should read: "The teacher will never give you punishment if you come on time." The other segments are correct: "the teacher will never" is a valid subject and verb phrase, "give you punishment" is acceptable (though "impose punishment" might be more formal), and "come on time" is grammatically sound.

p75mock010.explanation:

When cashiers and storekeepers cash up, they add up all the money taken from customers during a shift, or at the end of the working day. This phrasal verb does not fit in the given sentence which discusses that the cricket team had made no efforts towards a certain thing in World Cup.

'To cash in on' means 'to get money or another advantage from an event or situation, often in an unfair way'.

The phrase gives the meaning that the Indian cricket team did not unfairly use its vibrant image to get any advantage in the World Cup. It forms a meaningful sentence.

Hence, option a) is correct.

Note: Phrasal verb: A phrase that consists of a verb with a preposition or adverb or both, the meaning of which is different from the meaning of its separate parts. Example: She has always looked down on me. Here, the phrasal verb 'to look down on someone' doesn't mean that you are looking down from a higher place at someone who is below you; it means that you think that you are better than someone.

Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

They have been called off for now, so there is no guarantee they won't break out again.
p75mock011.explanation:
'Called off' is a phrasal verb which means to cancel something; to decide that something will not happen. 'Break out' is another phrasal verb which means start suddenly. So, the two clauses are contrasting in nature. We use 'so' as a subordinating conjunction to introduce clauses of result or decision which is not the case here.

For example: It was a long journey, so I'm really tired now.

Therefore, the underlined part is incorrect. Among the given options, 'but' is the most appropriate one as it can be used to connect ideas that are contrasting in nature. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

We use 'thus' to show that what you are about to mention is the result or consequence of something else that you have just mentioned. We use 'since' to give a reason for something.

Note:

Clause: A clause is a group of words that contains a verb (and usually other components too). A clause may form part of a sentence, or it may be a complete sentence in itself. Example:

1) "His products weren't selling"; this is an example of a sentence containing one clause.

2) "After we had had dinner, we went for a walk"; here, the sentence contains two clauses that are separated by a comma.

A clause can be categorised as:

1. Main/independent clause

2. Subordinate/dependent clause

Main/independent clause: In the example 2 given above, the clause "we went for a walk" can be said as the main clause (a clause that is not dependent on any other clause for its meaning, it makes sense on its own; a sentence contains at least one main clause.)

Subordinate/dependent clause: In example 2 given above, the clause "After we had had dinner" is a subordinate clause: it depends on the main clause for its meaning and cannot exist as a sentence on its own

CONJUNCTIONS

A conjunction (also called a connective) is a word such as and, because, but, for, if, or, when etc. Conjunctions are used to connect phrases, clauses, and sentences.

p75mock011.word:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

He picked up a vase from the table and flung it across the room.
options: A vase was picked up by him from the table and flung across the room.
A vase had been picked up by him from the table and flung across the room.
A vase was picked up by him from the table, and fling across the room.
A vase was being picked up by him from the table and flung across the room.
p75mock011.explanation:
The subject of the Active Voice is changed into the object of the Passive voice. Also, the object of the Active Voice is changed into the subject of the Passive Voice.

The Active voice in this question is in Past Indefinite. Thus, the Passive voice will also be in Past Indefinite.

The format of Active voice is: Subject + V2 + Object.

Thus, in Passive voice, the format will be: Subject (a vase) + was/were + V3 + by + Object (him).

Option b) is eliminated as it uses the past perfect tense.

Option c) is eliminated as it is grammatically incorrect; it changes the tense of the second verb (fling) into simple present tense.

Option d) is eliminated as it uses the past continuous tense, while the original sentence has used the simple past tense.

Hence, option a) is correct.

p75mock011.word:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The national anthem was being sung very enthusiastically by young students in the annual event.
options: The young students in the annual event were singing the national anthem very enthusiastically.
The national anthem was sung very enthusiastically for young students in the annual event.
The young students in the annual event had been singing the national anthem very enthusiastically.
The national anthem sang the young students very enthusiastically.
p75mock011.explanation:
The subject of the Passive Voice is changed into the object of the Active Voice. Also, the object of the Passive Voice is changed into the subject of the Active Voice.

The removal of the "to be" verb and the preposition 'by' is necessary while changing the voice of the sentence from Passive to Active.

The Passive voice in this question is in Past Continuous. Thus, the Active voice will also be in Past Continuous.

In Passive voice, the format is: Object of the Active voice (Subjective case) + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject of the Active voice (Objective case).

Thus, the format of Active voice is: Subject + was/were + V1 + ing + Object.

For example:

Math was being practised by Amit. (Passive Voice)

Amit was practising Math. (Active Voice)

The options except (a) don't follow the correct grammatical format of the Passive Voice.

Therefore, the correct answer is option (a): The young students in the annual event were singing the national anthem very enthusiastically.

p75mock011.word:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

She told her friends that she would be moving to a different state because she had accepted a job offer that required her to relocate.
options: She said to her friends, "I would have been moving to a different state because I had to accepted a job offer that requires me to relocate."
She said to her friends, "I was been moving to a different state because I have accepted a job offer that requires me to relocate."
She said to her friends, "I will be moving to a different state because I had have been accepted a job offer that requires me to relocate."
She said to her friends, "I will be moving to a different state because I have accepted a job offer that requires me to relocate."
p75mock011.explanation:
The initial part sentence in the Indirect Speech is in Present Conditional Tense. Therefore, the sentence in the Direct Speech will be in Future Simple Tense.

Present Conditional (Subject + would/should + V1 + object) will be converted into Future Simple (Subject + will/shall + V1 + object).

For example:

He said that he would go to Kolkata on Friday. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I will go to Kolkata on Friday" (Direct Speech)

For latter part-

Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 +Object) will be converted into Present Perfect (Subject + has/have + V3 +Object).

For example:

He said that he had got a new job. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I have got a new job." (Direct Speech)

Followed by the end part-

Simple Past (Subject + V2 + Object) will be converted into Simple Present (Subject + V1/V5 + Object).

For example:

He said that he wanted a new job. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I want a new job." (Direct Speech)

The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:

"would be" changes to "will be".

"Told" changes to "said to".

"she" changes to "I"

"Her" changes to "me"

"Had" changes to "have"

"Required" changes to "requires"

Therefore, the correct answer is: "She said to her friends, "I will be moving to a different state because I have accepted a job offer that requires me to relocate.""

Hence, option (d) is correct.

The subject of the Active Voice is changed into the object of the Passive voice. Also, the object of the Active Voice is changed into the subject of the Passive Voice.

The format of Active voice is: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object.

Thus, in Passive voice, the format will be: Object of the active voice (Subjective case) + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject of the active voice (Objective case).

For example:

Arya has bought a new horse. (Active Voice)

A new horse has been bought by Arya. (Passive Voice)

Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct speech.

Ruchi said that she was going to cast her vote.
options: Ruchi said to, "I was going to cast my vote".
Ruchi said, "I am going to cast my vote".
Ruchi said, "She was going to cast my vote".
Ruchi said, "I was going to cast her vote".
p75mock012.explanation:
The sentence in the Indirect Speech is in Past Continuous Tense. Therefore, the sentence in the Direct Speech will be in Present Continuous Tense.

Past Continuous (Subject + was/were + V1 + ing + Object) will be converted into Present Continuous (Subject + is/am/are + V1 +ing + Object)

For example:

He said that he was checking the assignment. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I am checking the assignment." (Direct Speech)

The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:

'She was' becomes 'I am', 'her' becomes 'my' and 'that' is removed.

Accordingly, the option that has the correct Direct speech sentence is (b), Ruchi said, "I am going to cast my vote".

Hence, the correct answer is option (b).

Note:

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

p75mock012.word:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in reported speech.

He said to me, "You would not live in peace if you did this to me."
options: He told me that I would not live in peace if I did that to him.
He told me that I would not live in peace if I had done that to him.
He told me that I would not live in peace if you had done that to me.
He told me that I could not live in peace if you had done that to me.
p75mock012.explanation:
The sentence in the Direct Speech is in Past Simple Tense. Therefore, the sentence in the Indirect Speech should be in Past Perfect Tense.

Past Simple (Subject + V2 + Object) should be converted into Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 + Object).

For example:

He said, "Arya sent me a book." (Direct Speech)

He said that Arya had sent him a book. (Indirect Speech)

When converting direct speech into indirect speech, the present modal verbs (should/might/could/would/ought to/had to) are not changed, and they remain the same in indirect speech.

Example: He said, "I should apologize to Jack for my bad behaviour." (Direct Speech)

He said that he should apologize to Jack for his bad behaviour". (Indirect Speech)

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:

· The pronoun 'you' and 'me' is changed into 'I' and 'him' respectively.

· The verb 'did' (past simple) is changed into 'had done' (past perfect).

· 'This' is changed into 'that' and 'said to' is changed into 'told'.

Therefore, the correct answer is option (b): He told me that I would not live in peace if I had done that to him.

p75mock012.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: Most of the candidates have submitted their digital applications online
and so the remaining offline applicants have in accordance
with the updated guidelines provided in the official recruitment notification.
No Error
p75mock012.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “the remaining offline applicants have” with “have the remaining offline applicants”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion after "So" in Affirmative Agreements

Positive statement :- SO+HV+SUB

When we want to avoid repeating a verb and express that a second subject has done the same thing as the first subject in an affirmative (positive) sentence, we use the structure: "So + Auxiliary Verb + Subject". This is a form of Partial Inversion where the auxiliary verb must precede the subject. The auxiliary verb must match the tense and aspect of the verb used in the first clause

💢 Application to the Given Question

...and so the remaining offline applicants have in accordance...

In the first part of the sentence, the auxiliary verb is "have" (Present Perfect). To show that the "remaining offline applicants" have also submitted their applications, we must use the inverted form after "so". Therefore, the auxiliary "have" must be placed before the subject "the remaining offline applicants".

Corrected Sentence

Most of the candidates have submitted their digital applications online and so have the remaining offline applicants in accordance with the updated guidelines provided in the official recruitment notification.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: Rahul loves playing chess, and so does his younger brother.

Example 2 ✅: The manager was impressed with the results, and so were the directors.

Example 3 ✅: I have finished my homework, and so has my roommate.

One of the first widely used wetland classifications systems, devised by Cowardin et al., 1979, categorized wetlands into marine (coastal wetlands), estuarine (including deltas, tidal marshes, and mangrove swamps), lacustrine (lakes), riverine (along rivers and streams), and palustrine ( marshes, swamps and bogs) based on their hydrological, ecological and geological characteristics.

Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was an international treaty signed in 1971. Overall, 1052 sites in Europe; 289 sites in Asia; 359 sites in Africa; 175 sites in South America; 211 sites in North America; and 79 sites in Oceania region have been identified as Ramsar sites or wetlands of International importance.

p75mock013.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: Following the alarming data breach, the cybersecurity
team investigated thoroughly the suspicious activity
detected within the encrypted servers.
No Error
p75mock013.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “investigated thoroughly the” with “investigated the suspicious activity thoroughly”.

Rule / Concept: Position of Adverb of Manner

An Adverb of Manner (which answers the question "How?") should generally be placed after the intransitive verb or after the direct object. Crucially, an adverb should never be placed between a transitive verb and its direct object.

Position of adverb of manner

Intransitive verbs:- After the main verb

Transitive verbs:- After the object ( If object is small.)

Transitive verbs:- Before the main verb

(If object is a noun clause.)

Application to the Given Question

"...the cybersecurity team investigated thoroughly the suspicious activity..."

In this sentence, "investigated" is a transitive verb and "the suspicious activity" is its direct object. Placing the adverb "thoroughly" between the verb and the object disrupts the flow of the sentence. The adverb must either come before the verb or, more commonly in exam patterns, after the entire object.

Corrected Sentence

Following the alarming data breach, the cybersecurity team investigated the suspicious activity thoroughly within the encrypted servers. (Alternatively: "...thoroughly investigated the suspicious activity...")

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: She speaks English well. (Verb + Object + Adverb) ✅

Example 2: He ate the chocolate greedily. (Verb + Object + Adverb) ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1: She speaks well English. ❌

Wrong example 2: He ate greedily the chocolate. ❌

hings to Remember / Exam Tips

  • Spotting the Object: Always identify if the verb has an object. If you see "Verb + Adverb + Noun," check if that noun is the object of the verb. If it is, the adverb is likely misplaced.

  • Intransitive Exception: If there is no object, the adverb immediately follows the verb (e.g., "He walked slowly").

Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The contract will have been signed by the partners by next Friday.
options: The partners will have signed the contract by next Friday.
The partners will sign the contract by next Friday.
The partners will be signing the contract by next Friday.
The partners would sign the contract by next Friday.
p75mock014.explanation:
The subject of the Passive Voice is changed into the object of the Active Voice. Also, the object of the Passive Voice is changed into the subject of the Active Voice.

The removal of the "to be" verb (been) and the preposition "by" is necessary while changing the voice of the sentence from Passive to Active.

The Passive voice in this question is in Future Perfect. Thus, the Active voice will also be in Future Perfect.

In Passive voice, the format is: Object of the Active voice (Subjective case) + will/shall + have + been + V3 + by + Subject of the Active voice (Objective case)

Thus, the format of Active voice is: Subject + will/shall + have + V3 + Object.

For example:

The gold will have been bought by her. (Passive Voice)

She will have bought the gold. (Active Voice)

The options except (a) don't follow the correct grammatical format of the Active Voice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: The partners will have signed the contract by next Friday.

p75mock014.word: Choose the correct Active/Passive sentence:
options: Due to cold weather, the vehicles were by the authorities.
The authorities stopped the vehicles due to cold weather.
The authorities stopped due to the cold weather.
The cold weather stopped due to the authorities.
p75mock014.explanation:
In an active voice sentence, the following format can be seen 'Subject + Verb (tense may vary) + Object'. For a passive voice sentence, the format is 'Subject (objective case of Active voice) + Verb (based on tense in Active voice) + by + Object (subjective case of the Active voice)'.

Among the given options, the only sentence that appropriately follows the grammatical rules of an Active voice sentence is option (b), 'The authorities stopped the vehicles due to cold weather'.

Options (a), (c) and (d) do not comply with the grammatical requirements of an Active or Passive voice sentence and thus they are negated.

Hence, the correct answer is option (b).

Note:

Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).

B. I need to have homework before going out to meet my friends.

C. I need to done homework before going out to meet my friends.

D. I need to do homework before going out to meet mine friends.
p75mock014.explanation:
Sentence A correctly uses the phrase "do homework" and is grammatically correct. The phrase "do homework" is appropriate for expressing the need to complete tasks. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

B- The phrase "have homework" suggests possessing or being assigned homework, rather than completing it, which is incorrect meaningfully.

C- The phrase "to done" is incorrect. The correct form should be "to do", as the infinitive marker "to" should be followed by the base verb ['Done' is V2/V3].

D- The possessive pronoun "mine" is used without a following noun. Here, since the noun follows it, it should be replaced with "my" (possessive determiner).

Note: Possessive Determiners/Adjectives: Words like 'my', 'our', 'your', 'his', 'her', 'its', and 'their' are known as possessive adjectives (or possessive determiners). They come before nouns and indicate ownership of the noun. Example: "The teacher asked the students to open their drawing books."

Possessive Pronouns: The pronouns mine, yours, hers, his, ours, and theirs are known as possessive pronouns: they refer to something owned by the speaker or by someone or something previously mentioned. For example: The pen is mine.

Infinitive marker: A word or affix attached to the stem of a verb in order to form the full infinitive. In English, to is the infinitive marker.

every individual present in the high-security
zone undergoes a thorough biometric screening.

📌 Rule / Concept: The "Until/Unless" Rule (Time & Conditional Clauses)

When a sentence refers to two actions in the future, we use the Future Tense (will + V1) in the main clause, but we never use "will" in the subordinate clause introduced by time or condition conjunctions like if, when, until, unless, before, after, or as soon as. Instead, we use the Simple Present Tense

💢 Application to the Given Question

"...protocols will remain... until every individual... undergoes..."

This sentence correctly follows the rule:

  1. Main Clause: "The security protocols will remain in effect" correctly uses the Future Tense to describe the ongoing state.

  2. Time Clause: "until every individual... undergoes..." correctly uses the Simple Present (V{s/es}) following the conjunction "until."

Even though the "undergoing" of screening will happen in the future, the grammar requires the Simple Present because "until" establishes the boundary/condition for the main action.

p75mock019.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

in the train which met
with an accident last night.
No error
p75mock019.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “They were luckily” with “Luckily, they were”

Concept: Placement of "Sentence Adverbs"

There are certain adverbs (like luckily, fortunately, happily, surprisingly, honestly) that modify the entire sentence or the speaker’s attitude toward the situation, rather than just the verb. These are called Sentence Adverbs.

  • Rule: When an adverb modifies the whole sentence, it should ideally be placed at the very beginning of the sentence, followed by a comma.

  • The Trap: If you place "luckily" after the verb "were," it suggests that the manner of their being was lucky, which is awkward. We want to say that the entire situation (them not being on the train) was a piece of good luck.

Application to the Given Question

The sentence describes a fortunate escape from a train accident. The "luck" doesn't apply to the action of traveling; it applies to the fact that they happened to be elsewhere.

  • Incorrect: They were luckily not travelling... (This incorrectly tries to modify the verb phrase).

  • Correct: Luckily, they were not travelling... (This modifies the whole fact that they weren't on the train).

Corrected Sentence

Luckily, they were not travelling in the train which met with an accident last night.

More Examples for Clarity

  1. Fortunately: Fortunately, the fire was extinguished before it reached the kitchen.

  2. Honestly: Honestly, I don't know the answer to your question.

  3. Surprisingly: Surprisingly, the team won despite having no experience.

NOTE:

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

📌Rule/Concept: Direct Objects with Transitive Reporting Verbs -

Certain verbs are transitive, meaning they require a direct object to complete their meaning. The verb 'Ask', when used to mean "requesting someone" or "questioning someone," is a transitive verb. Therefore, it is followed immediately by the person (the object) without the preposition 'to'.

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, "the candidates" is the direct object of the verb "asked." Adding the preposition "to" between a transitive verb and its direct object is a grammatical redundancy. Just as we do not say "He told to me, "we must not say "He asked to me." The preposition "to" is only used with "ask" in very specific, rare idioms (like "ask to see"), but never when placed before the person being addressed

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

The "Tell" Rule: Treat "Ask" like "Tell." You say "Tell him," not "Tell to him." Similarly, use "Ask him," not "Ask to him."

Direct vs. Indirect: "Ask" is followed by the person (Direct Object). The preposition "to" usually appears after the person to introduce the infinitive verb (e.g., Asked him to go).

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1: I asked him to finish the report by Friday afternoon. Example 2: The teacher asked the students to submit their assignments. Example 3: Did you ask the supervisor for permission to leave early?

p75mock023.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: In case if it rains,
I will take
an umbrella.
No Error
p75mock023.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option A

👉 Replace “In case if” with “In case” or “If”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Redundancy / Superfluous Expressions

In formal English grammar, redundancy occurs when two words or phrases with the same meaning are used together. Both "In case" and "If" are conjunctions used to introduce a condition or a contingency. Using them simultaneously creates a "superfluous" error because one word makes the other unnecessary.

In case: Used to talk about precautions (doing something because something else might happen).

If: Used to talk about a condition (doing something only if something else happens).

✅ Corrected Sentence

In case it rains, I will take an umbrella. (OR)

If it rains, I will take an umbrella.

❌ Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1 ❌: Suppose if you win the lottery, how will you spend the money?

Wrong example 2 ❌: We will stay indoors in case if the storm gets worse.

Replace “their” with “theirs”

Rule / Concept: Possessive Adjectives vs. Possessive Pronouns

Possessive Adjectives (my, our, your, his, her, its, their) must always be followed by a noun because they function as modifiers (e.g., their strategy). Possessive Pronouns (mine, ours, yours, his, hers, its, theirs) stand alone and replace the "Possessive Adjective + Noun" structure to avoid repetition. They never take a noun after them.

NOTE: POSSESSIVE PRONOUN = POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE + NOUN

Example: yours = your + dog (noun)

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, there is no noun following the word "their." Since the sentence is referring to "the creative department's concept" without repeating the word "concept," a possessive pronoun is required. "Their" is an adjective and cannot stand alone; "theirs" is the correct pronoun.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

-The Noun Check: Always look at what follows the word. If there is a noun (e.g., their house), use the adjective. If there is a verb or a full stop (e.g., is theirs.), use the pronoun.

-The "s" Factor: Except for "mine," most possessive pronouns end in "s" (ours, yours, hers, theirs).

-Avoid the Apostrophe: Never use an apostrophe with possessive pronouns (theirs, NOT their's).

Mental health has increasingly entered public discourse, yet its inclusion often remains superficial rather than transformative. Awareness campaigns proliferate, terminology becomes more familiar, and institutions adopt symbolic gestures of concern. However, beneath this apparent progress lies a persistent reluctance to confront the structural and cultural conditions that generate psychological distress. Mental health is frequently treated as an individual malfunction, detached from social environments that normalize chronic stress, insecurity, and emotional suppression. This individualized framing carries subtle consequences. When distress is reduced to personal resilience or chemical imbalance, responsibility quietly shifts away from workplaces, educational systems, and economic arrangements that perpetuate exhaustion and precarity. Coping mechanisms are emphasized over prevention, and adaptation is rewarded more than dissent. In such a framework, the mentally healthy individual is not one who is free from distress, but one who can continue functioning despite it. Institutional responses often mirror this logic. Support systems exist, but access is conditional, fragmented, and reactive. Interventions are triggered once productivity declines or visible crisis emerges, rather than when early signs of strain appear. Moreover, the language of wellness is frequently co-opted to enhance performance rather than well-being, blurring the line between care and control. Key Points

  • The "It is time" Rule: This phrase is an idiomatic expression that is always followed by the Simple Past tense (e.g., started) to show that an action is overdue.

  • Main Clause Shift: The introductory part "It is time" must shift back one step to "It was time" because the reporting verb ("said") is in the past tense.

  • The "No Change" Exception: While standard narration rules usually shift Simple Past to Past Perfect, the verb following "It is time" is an exception. It stays in the Simple Past (started) to maintain the specific meaning of the idiom.

    • Note: If you change it to "had started," the sentence loses its idiomatic meaning of "urgency".

  • Pronoun Change: The second-person pronoun "you" refers to the son, so it changes to "he" in indirect speech.

p75mock026.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: The management is actively seeking an experienced marketing
executive who he can represent the company at
the upcoming international trade summit in Delhi.
No Error
p75mock026.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “who he can” with “who can”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Redundancy of the Personal Pronoun (The Double Subject)

A Relative Pronoun (who, which, that, whom) serves two purposes:

-It acts as a conjunction joining two clauses.

-It acts as a pronoun replacing the noun (antecedent) in the second clause.

When the relative pronoun is used as the subject of the subordinate clause, you must not use another personal pronoun (he, she, it, they) for the same verb. Doing so creates a "double subject" error

Application to the Given Question

"...marketing executive who he can represent the company..."

-Antecedent: Marketing executive

-Relative Pronoun: Who (refers back to the executive)

-Verb: Can represent

In this structure, "who" is already the subject of the verb "can represent." Adding "he" is redundant because both words are trying to perform the same function for the same verb. It is like saying, "Rajat he is going to Delhi."

Corrected Sentence - The management is actively seeking an experienced marketing executive who can represent the company at the upcoming international trade summit in Delhi.

More Examples for Clarity

-Example 1: The book which it is on the table is mine. ❌

-Correction: The book which is on the table is mine. ✅

-Example 2: Those people who they work hard succeed in life. ❌

-Correction: Those people who work hard succeed in life. ✅

-Example 3: This is the car that it broke down yesterday. ❌

-Correction: This is the car that broke down yesterday. ✅

The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

The error is in the part "to stay back after office hours". Certain verbs like 'make', 'let', 'help', and 'bid', when used in the active voice, are followed by a bare infinitive (the base form of a verb without 'to'). In this sentence, 'made' is used in the active voice.

Therefore, the infinitive marker 'to' should be removed before the verb 'stay'. The correct phrase is "stay back".

Correct Sentence: The manager made the new intern stay back after office hours to finish the urgent report.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

Note:

· Infinitive: The infinitive is the base form of a verb, often preceded by to.

Consider the sentences given below:

· To err is human. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to err' is the subject of the verb 'is']

· My father likes to cook. [like a noun, the infinitive 'to cook' is the object of the verb 'likes']

· To vote in elections is our right. [the infinitive 'to vote', like a noun, is the subject of the verb 'is', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (elections)]

· Radha went to the lake to fetch water. [the infinitive 'to fetch', like a noun, is the object of the verb 'went', but, like a verb, it also takes an object (water)]

· The above sentences illustrate various ways in which infinitives are used. It can both act as a noun and a verb.

· Infinitive marker: A word or affix attached to the stem of a verb in order to form the full infinitive. In English, to is the infinitive marker.

· Active and Passive Voice: When the person doing the action is the subject, the sentence is said to be in active form/voice. When the subject is what the action is directed at, then the sentence is said to be in passive form/voice. For example: Active Voice: Rita and her friends performed a skit. Here 'Rita and her friends' (subject) perform the action. Passive Voice: A skit was performed by Rita and her friends. Here 'skit' is the subject (at which the action is directed).

Jim said that I will join the office soon.
p75mock027.explanation:
The sentence in the Direct Speech is in Future Simple Tense. Therefore, the sentence in the Indirect Speech should be in Present Conditional Tense.

Future Simple (Subject + will/shall + V1 + object) should be converted into Present Conditional (Subject + would/should + V1 +object).

For example:

He said, "I will be in Kolkata on Friday." (Direct Speech)

He said that he would be in Kolkata on Friday. (Indirect Speech)

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech: 'I' becomes 'he', 'will' becomes 'would', and 'that' gets included.

Accordingly, the correct form of Indirect speech for the sentence is given in option (c), Jim said that he would join the office soon.

Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

Note:

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

p75mock027.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: My youngest brother, who recently
graduated from the prestigious law school,
he is now practicing in the High Court.
p75mock027.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “he is now” with “is now”.

Rule / Concept: The Redundant Subject

a sentence should have only one subject for a single predicate (action). A common error occurs when a noun subject is introduced, followed by a relative clause (like who..., which..., that...), and then a pronoun (like he, she, it) is added before the main verb.

Since the noun at the beginning is already the subject of the main verb, the pronoun is unnecessary and grammatically incorrect.

💢 Application to the Given Question

Let's look at the "skeleton" of the sentence:

"My youngest brother (Subject)... is now practicing (Verb)."

Now, look at how the error is inserted:

"My youngest brother (A), who recently graduated from (B) the prestigious law school, he is now (C)..."

  1. The subject is "My youngest brother".

  2. The phrase "who recently graduated... school" is an adjective clause giving more info about the brother.

  3. The word "he" is a pronoun referring back to the brother.

Because "My youngest brother" is already waiting to perform the action "is practicing," adding "he" creates a Double Subject. You must delete the pronoun.

Corrected Sentence "My youngest brother, who recently graduated from the prestigious law school, is now practicing in the High Court."

Mental health has increasingly entered public discourse, yet its inclusion often remains superficial rather than transformative. Awareness campaigns proliferate, terminology becomes more familiar, and institutions adopt symbolic gestures of concern. However, beneath this apparent progress lies a persistent reluctance to confront the structural and cultural conditions that generate psychological distress. Mental health is frequently treated as an individual malfunction, detached from social environments that normalize chronic stress, insecurity, and emotional suppression. This individualized framing carries subtle consequences. When distress is reduced to personal resilience or chemical imbalance, responsibility quietly shifts away from workplaces, educational systems, and economic arrangements that perpetuate exhaustion and precarity. Coping mechanisms are emphasized over prevention, and adaptation is rewarded more than dissent. In such a framework, the mentally healthy individual is not one who is free from distress, but one who can continue functioning despite it. Institutional responses often mirror this logic. Support systems exist, but access is conditional, fragmented, and reactive. Interventions are triggered once productivity declines or visible crisis emerges, rather than when early signs of strain appear. Moreover, the language of wellness is frequently co-opted to enhance performance rather than well-being, blurring the line between care and control. As a result, mental health initiatives risk becoming tools for sustaining existing norms rather than questioning them. The deeper challenge, therefore, lies in redefining mental health beyond the absence of disorder. It demands recognition of emotional suffering as a rational response to irrational conditions. Without this shift, societies may continue to expand mental health services while simultaneously reproducing the very pressures that make such services indispensable.

p75mock032.word: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options: In order to maintain a healthy work-life
balance, many successful entrepreneurs avoid
to check their emails after midnight.
p75mock032.explanation:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “to check” with “checking”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Verbs followed by Gerunds

n English, certain verbs are transitively followed by a Gerund (V{ing}) rather than an Infinitive (to + V1). The verb "Avoid" is a prime example. When we use "avoid," the action that follows must be in the noun-form (Gerund) to complete the meaning of the sentence. Using an infinitive after "avoid" is grammatically incorrect in formal English.

💢 Application to the Given Question

"...many successful entrepreneurs avoid to check their emails..."

In this sentence, the verb "avoid" is the main action. The secondary action, which is the act of checking emails, must be expressed as a Gerund. Therefore, the infinitive "to check" must be changed to the gerund "checking" to satisfy the grammatical requirement of the verb "avoid."

Corrected Sentence

In order to maintain a healthy work-life balance, many successful entrepreneurs avoid checking their emails after midnight.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ You should avoid making hasty decisions during a crisis.

Example 2 ✅ Most people detest waiting in long queues at the billing counter.

Example 3 ✅ The committee suggested implementing the new policy immediately.

REMEMBAER THE LIST

Verbs that are followed by gerund:- detest, mind, resent, avoid, Stop, excuse, resist, miss, prevent, defer, delay, postpone, consider, risk

appreciate, admire, forget, forgive, recollect, remember, suggest, etc

p75mock033.word: Select the grammatically correct sentence.
options: They have know each other since childhood.
Arnav has lived in this city for ten years.
We have just move into our new house.
They had buy tickets for the concert, but it was cancelled at the last minute.
p75mock033.explanation:
The sentence given in option (b) is grammatically correct.

Option (a) is not correct. In the present perfect tense (indicated by the helping verb 'have'), the correct form of the main verb after "have" is the past participle form. But 'know' (base form) is not the past participle form of the verb. Accordingly, 'know' should be replaced with the past participle form 'known'. The correct sentence is: They have known each other since childhood.

Option (c) is incorrect. In the present perfect tense (indicated by the helping verb 'have'), the correct form of the main verb after "have" is the past participle form. But 'move' (base form) is not the past participle form of the verb. Accordingly, 'move' should be replaced with the past participle form 'moved'. The correct sentence is: We have just moved into our new house.

Option (d) is also incorrect. In the past perfect tense (indicated by the helping verb 'had'), the correct form of the main verb after "had" is the past participle form. But the verb "buy" (base form) is not the past participle form of the verb. Accordingly, 'buy' should be replaced with the past participle form 'bought'. Also, "had bought" is used to indicate an action that occurred before another action in the past (in this case, the cancellation of the concert).

The correct sentence is: They had bought tickets for the concert, but it was cancelled at the last minute. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

NOTE:

Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.

p75mock033.word:
Mental health has increasingly entered public discourse, yet its inclusion often remains superficial rather than transformative. Awareness campaigns proliferate, terminology becomes more familiar, and institutions adopt symbolic gestures of concern. However, beneath this apparent progress lies a persistent reluctance to confront the structural and cultural conditions that generate psychological distress. Mental health is frequently treated as an individual malfunction, detached from social environments that normalize chronic stress, insecurity, and emotional suppression. This individualized framing carries subtle consequences. When distress is reduced to personal resilience or chemical imbalance, responsibility quietly shifts away from workplaces, educational systems, and economic arrangements that perpetuate exhaustion and precarity. Coping mechanisms are emphasized over prevention, and adaptation is rewarded more than dissent. In such a framework, the mentally healthy individual is not one who is free from distress, but one who can continue functioning despite it. Institutional responses often mirror this logic. Support systems exist, but access is conditional, fragmented, and reactive. Interventions are triggered once productivity declines or visible crisis emerges, rather than when early signs of strain appear. Moreover, the language of wellness is frequently co-opted to enhance performance rather than well-being, blurring the line between care and control. As a result, mental health initiatives risk becoming tools for sustaining existing norms rather than questioning them. The deeper challenge, therefore, lies in redefining mental health beyond the absence of disorder. It demands recognition of emotional suffering as a rational response to irrational conditions. Without this shift, societies may continue to expand mental health services while simultaneously reproducing the very pressures that make such services indispensable.

Which of the following can be most reasonably inferred from the passage?
options: Expanding mental health services alone may not reduce psychological distress
Chemical treatment is ineffective in addressing mental health issues
Institutions deliberately ignore mental health concerns
Emotional suffering is always caused by personal weakness
p75mock033.explanation:
The Correct Answer is - Expanding mental health services alone may not reduce psychological distress.

Explanation:
The passage implies that without addressing structural and cultural causes, increased services merely manage symptoms. This inference aligns with the critique of reactive and surface-level responses.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG:

C attributes intent where the passage discusses systemic patterns.

p75mock034.word:
Renewable energy is often presented as an uncomplicated remedy to the twin crises of climate change and energy insecurity. Governments announce ambitious targets, corporations highlight sustainability commitments, and public discourse treats renewables as an inevitable successor to fossil fuels. Yet this narrative of inevitability conceals a more complex reality. Transitioning to renewable energy is not merely a technological substitution but a structural transformation involving land use, grid stability, economic redistribution, and political negotiation. Ignoring these dimensions risks replacing one form of dependency with another. One persistent challenge lies in intermittency. Solar and wind energy, while abundant, are not continuously available, requiring storage systems or backup infrastructure. Although technological advances have reduced costs, large-scale storage remains economically and logistically constrained. As a result, renewable integration often relies on conventional energy sources during periods of low generation. This dependence complicates claims of energy independence and exposes the limits of viewing renewables as a standalone solution.

Social and environmental trade-offs further complicate the transition. Large renewable projects demand vast land areas, sometimes displacing communities or disrupting local ecosystems. Transparent governance, adaptive grid management, and equitable distribution of costs and benefits are critical. 📌 Rule / Concept: Present Perfect with Ordinal Phrase

When a sentence uses an introductory phrase like "This is the first/second/third time...", "This is the best/worst...", or "This is the only...", it implies that an experience started in the past and is being completed or counted at the present moment.   • Incorrect: ...the third time the server crashed (Simple Past suggests the month is over).

  • Correct: ...the third time the server has crashed (Connects the event to the current "third" instance).

This is the third time this month that the server of our main branch has crashed unexpectedly, resulting in a significant loss of productivity for the technical department.
